pairs.subject: runner-fleet
pairs.evidence: crates/runner/src/dispatch.rs:49 lt-runner is an application job worker. It claims evaluation jobs (BenchRun, ScoreEvents, ScoreTraces, DatasetSample, Calibrate, Contribute) from LightTrack's own API, and it is not a CI/delivery runner that executes builds or deploys; a case-insensitive search of crates/runner for runs-on, self-hosted, actions/cache, sccache and autoscal found nothing, so the subject's precondition (a fleet of machines executing delivery work) does not hold here, and the subject itself hands generic work coordination to job-coordination.

techniques.evidence: crates/runner/src/serve.rs:31 This looks like the same idea at the application level: workers declare kinds and providers (serve.rs:33-35, providers_from_env). But it routes app jobs, not CI capabilities, so the technique does not govern it.
crates/runner/src/serve.rs:111 A single process polls at a fixed interval. Nothing in this context provisions or scales runner capacity.

pairs.registryProposal: The registry map paired runner-fleet with this context, probably because the crate and binary are named 'runner'. An application background-job worker is governed by job-coordination/background-jobs, not by a CI runner fleet. Still, capability-typed-queues has a real application-level analog here: workers declare the kinds and providers they can handle, and a request nobody can satisfy queues and is surfaced to the operator rather than failed. That rule may be worth stating in background-jobs or job-coordination.
